title: Crusoe walks away from $1.25B Boom Supersonic turbine deal for AI data centres
subtitle: The Denver-based operator was to be the launch customer for 29 of Boom's 42MW natural-gas 'Superpower' turbines — Crusoe has now shifted to GE Vernova and Bergen Engines and stepped back from a Wyoming gigawatt-scale campus.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Crusoe, the Denver AI data-centre operator that raised $3.9 billion earlier this year, cancelled its $1.25 billion contract with Boom Supersonic to buy 29 of Boom's new 42-megawatt stationary natural-gas turbines — 1.21GW of nameplate capacity in total. Boom had positioned Crusoe as the launch customer for the 'Superpower' units, with first deliveries slated for 2027. Boom CEO Blake Scholl confirmed the change and said the company still plans to deliver roughly 250MW of the turbines to other sites next year. Crusoe has instead ordered about 1GW of generation equipment from GE Vernova and signed a separate contract with Bergen Engines. The company has also stepped back from a previously announced gigawatt-scale AI campus in Wyoming.

This matters because Crusoe has been one of the loudest voices in the 'behind-the-meter' AI-power thesis — the idea that frontier compute needs its own generation on the site of the data centre, not the grid. Committing to 29 supersonic-derivative turbines from a company whose main business is airplanes was the boldest expression of that thesis on the market. Reversing it means Crusoe is choosing conventional, proven generation from known suppliers and a more modular footprint over one giant custom bet, and the biggest AI-infrastructure buyer of the year now believes that flexibility is worth more than nameplate MWs signed years in advance.

The broader question is whether other operators follow. The $50B+ hyperscaler pipeline — Meta's Louisiana Hyperion, Microsoft's 26GW 2032 target, xAI's Colossus 2 doubling in Memphis, Anthropic's Volta/Bitdeer Norway build — all lock in gigawatts of power years before the compute is landed. Every one of those commitments carries the same risk Crusoe just took off the table: the specific power hardware you signed for in 2026 may not be the hardware you actually want to run in 2028. Boom's turbines were never delivered, so Crusoe took a smaller write-down than the full contract value, but the message to the rest of the market is clear.

For learners: when a large infrastructure buyer walks away from a headline deal, the story that matters is not the cancellation itself — it's the substitution. Crusoe did not stop building; it switched to suppliers that already ship at scale. Watch for the same pattern with GPU commitments over the next twelve months. Contracts that name a specific accelerator generation two years out will start to be renegotiated, and the winners will be vendors whose supply is already in production, not those with the best projected specs.
